name: Beth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate French into English, mainly for a church mission charity that works with partner churches in West Africa. Three days a week I turn their field reports, prayer letters and funding applications into English. The other two days I take freelance jobs, mostly shipping papers and contracts for a cocoa importer near the docks. I work from the back bedroom of the house we rent, while my husband Kwame is out on jobs as an electrician.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is a report from a village pastor about a new well, and knowing my English is what gets it funded. The hard part is that the charity's donations are down and they've warned us all about cuts in the spring. We've less than a month's money saved, and we were hoping to start a family next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that good writing still needs a person behind it. At church I'd say it's a reminder not to put our faith in machines. I'd probably not say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it doesn't fix the charity's money problem. Donations are falling anyway, and if they cut my days, I'm down to two days of cocoa contracts. That worries me more than AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my three days and ask the cocoa importer for more regular work, maybe a set number of contracts a month. I already use the translation tool now and then for rough drafts of the long reports; I'd keep doing that to save time. And Kwame and I would hold off on the baby until the spring cuts are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not AI that worries me in this one, it's the charity's budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on a baby is a big decision. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Kwame would say God provides, and I'd say God also gave us a calculator. We'd agree to wait until summer and pray about it. We've had that talk before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the translation tool for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A forty-page annual report from Cameroon, say. I'd let the tool do a rough version, then rewrite every page so it sounds like the pastor, not a manual. It saves me a day, which I can then give to the cocoa contracts.

feel: **Uneasy** about the charity's budget, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and we adjust, as people always have. I'd tell friends at church that the trades are a good bet, like Kwame's. I don't like complaining about it; that's not how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the charity would use AI for its reports and keep one person to check them, probably not me. The cocoa contracts would go the same way. I'd still have work, but less and less of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into training as a French teacher, since schools still need someone in the room with the children. In the first year I'd do a teaching assistant job at the church primary school if they'd have me. I'd learn the AI tools properly too, once I saw other translators making them work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed more than scared. Kwame's work is steady, so we wouldn't starve, but my part of the money would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching, rather than staying in translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I love the language, but I don't love sitting alone with a screen. A room full of eight-year-olds saying 'bonjour' badly is better than most days at my desk. And I'd want those hours when we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the charity would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Adjei, who's run the translation side for twenty years. She's 61 and has nothing else. I'd worry about her more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to pull together. I'm not one to ask the government for much, but two years is too fast for people to manage alone. I'd say it at church and to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my translation work would be gone within a year of it arriving. It's all writing and checking; there's no hands-on part. The robots in 2031 matter more for Kwame, because his electrical work has those three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight for any job at the church school, even lunchtime cover, to have a foot in. We'd cut everything and save on Kwame's wage. We'd put the baby off for at least two years, which would break my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And sad, because we'd planned our life around starting a family soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kwame has three extra years. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe by then people still want a real electrician they can trust in their house. We'd have to pray and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would tell me to come and stay with her and save the rent. She's in a two-bedroom flat across town. Kwame would hate it, but we might have to.

**Two years** is too fast for people to manage alone, even with family.
think: My **translation work** would be gone within a year.
The **robot delay** matters more for Kwame's electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if families plan together. I'd tell young people at church to think hard before studying languages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three good years from the charity and the cocoa firm. That's long enough to train as a teacher. I'd still lose translation, but I'd land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time teacher training course in the first year while keeping my three charity days. We'd save a bit from both wages. And we'd probably still try for a baby next year, because five years is time to plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. This version I can manage with God's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell young people not to study languages? That's a big thing to say.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not exactly. Language on its own, sitting at a screen, is what goes first. I'd tell young people to learn a language and a trade. Or a language and teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss from translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pastors' letters, really. Reading how a village celebrated a new school roof. I'd miss being the voice for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it wisely. I'd tell people not to panic and not to wait either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have most of a decade of translation, with less each year. I'd be a teacher by the end, and Kwame's work lasts until about 2039. We'd be all right, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and start teacher training in a year or two. We'd have our first child as we'd planned. I'd use the AI tools more, since they'd be proven, so I could do more work in fewer hours with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace. A bit unsettled, but I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI more with a baby. Doesn't that hurry along the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but using the tools isn't me deciding the future, it's me feeding my family. One translator not using the tools won't stop anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: French, from me, at the kitchen table. And a proper trade, from their dad. Then they've got both.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would take my work just as we wanted a baby. What would help is a paid route into teaching for people my age, and some help for families starting out, through churches and local groups.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. People think faith is just comfort, but faith is also how you decide what matters when everything changes. For us, that's family first.

headlineQuote: People think faith is just comfort, but faith is also how you decide what matters when everything changes.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** French–English translator for a church mission charity and a cocoa importer.
She's married to Kwame, an **electrician**, and they hope to start a family soon.
She uses AI **now and then** for rough drafts of long reports.
Traditional and faithful, she relies on **family and church** before the state.
Across scenarios she plans a move into **teaching**, with the baby's timing as the real stake.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would take her work just as they want a baby.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid route into teaching** for people her age.
Help for **young families** through churches and local groups.
